title: WPSS/2384/2018 of REENA ALVI Vs STATE OF UTTARAKHAND THROUGH SECRETARY, SECONDARY EDUCATION

paras.text:
IN HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Writ Petition No.2384 of 2018 (S/S)
Reena Alvi (Female) .....Petitioner
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand and others ...Respondents
Advocate: Mr. Sandeep Tiwari, Advocate for the petitioner.
 Mr. N.P. Sah, Standing Counsel for the State of Uttarakhand.
 Mr. Pankaj Purohit, Advocate for respondent no. 2.
 Mr. Mohd. Umar, Advocate for respondent no.3.

Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.
Brief facts of the case are that the respondent no.2 herein i.e.
Uttarakhand Subordinate Service Selection Commission had resorted to the
process of recruitment for Group 'C' post by inviting the applications from
the prospective candidates to filled in 1546 post of Group 'C' employees,
which was made available at the relevant point of time, and in relation thereto
they had issued an advertisement on 03.01.2017. On the scrutiny of the
advertisement itself and even if it is taken into consideration from the
prospective of the recruitment process, which has been resorted to though it
relates to the different departments of the state services, for which the
vacancies were consolidated together and advertised for resorting to the
process of selection, but invariably if the classification of the vacancies is
taken into consideration, as provided respectively in its Clause 3, the entire
vacancies which were thus advertised on 03.01.2017, was for the candidates
from amongst the general category candidates no reserved category candidate
vacancies were advertised for the selection process.
2. Under a normal analogy where there happens to be an
advertisement which is exclusively for the selection process for general
category candidate, it does not de-bars the candidate belonging to reserve
category to apply for extension of his/her candidature to be considered for
recruitment against the general category candidate, as advertised in the instant
case. But in that eventuality the reserved category candidate, though can

2
participate in the selection process on the posts advertised for general
candidates, but on extension of his or her candidature, no benefit or
relaxation, which is otherwise available to a reserved category as per law,
could be claimed to be extended, when the reserved category candidate
applies for selection against the post made available for the general category
only. Few facts, which are not disputed are that:-
1. That the petitioner belongs to the OBC category of reserved
category.
2. But, however, the petitioner had voluntarily extended her
candidature, while responding to the Advertisement No.08 dated
03.01.2017; to be considered for appointment against the vacancies
had been exclusively made available for general category.
3. It is not a fact which has been disputed, that the petitioner had
procured 50% marks in her TET examination.
4. It is further not in dispute even that in the advertisement dated
03.01.2017, it was exclusively a recruitment exercise, which was to
be taken for the general category only, as no OBC posts were
included or advertised to be filled in, in the aforesaid process of
selection.
5. Petitioner participated in the process of selection as resorted to; in
pursuance to the said application by submitting her application form
on 22.01.2017, to be considered against general category post, much
before the cut off date provided in the advertisement for applying
i.e. 12.03.2017.
3. The petitioner submits, that after scrutinization of her
testimonials and the documents filed in support of her application, that was
scrutinized by the respondents and based on the educational qualification
possessed by her, she was issued with an admit card and she had participated
in the written examination which was conducted by the respondents on
21.01.2008. But, however in the provisional merit list, which was thus issued
by respondent no.2 on 19.07.2018, the petitioner's name was not included in
the said select list and hence the petitioner had raised a grievance by

3
contending thereof; that once she has qualified on the basis of the marks
procured by her to be appointed based on her placement in the select list too
as amongst the vacancies, which were advertised for the general category
candidate; her name ought to have been included in the provisional merit list
as notified on 19.07.2018 and hence, she has sought for; that after including
her name in the merit list of 19.07.2018, a writ of mandamus may be issued to
the respondents to consider the candidature of the petitioner for recruitment
as an Assistant Teacher LT Grade (Urdu) in the Kumaun Region, from
amongst the General Uttarakhand Woman category.
4. But however, the candidature of the petitioner as per the counter
affidavit filed by the respondents was declined to be included in the merit
select list for the reason being, that according to the cut off marks, which a
general category candidate was required to possess for the purposes of
considering of his/her candidature for being appointed from amongst the
general category candidate, it was 60% marks in the TET. Admittedly, the
petitioner was having only 50% of marks, though she might have been the
applicant to be considered, as against the general category candidate which
were advertised and was placed on the merit list but her candidature was
rejected on the ground that since she was not having the 60% TET marks,
which was the cut off, she was held to be not eligible to be included in the
select list.
5. The argument of the learned counsel for the petitioner is that
even if the petitioner had admittedly applied as against the general category
candidate, in response to the advertisement, which was issued by the
respondents on 03.01.2017, and she had voluntarily extended her candidature
for being considered against the post made available for the general category
candidate. In that eventuality too, the contention of the learned counsel for the
petitioner is that under the normal parameters prescribed by respondent no.2,
in order to make an OBC category candidate eligible to be consider for
appointment by providing cut off mark of 50%, it ought to have taken as to be
the basis for inclusion of the name of the petitioner in the select list, which
was published by the respondent on 19.07.2018.

4
6. This contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner is
strongly refuted by the respondents on the ground, that prescription of 50% of
cut off marks for an OBC category candidate is only available to be applied,
when who applies as an OBC category candidate for the post which it is
included in the advertisement, it would only be available, when her
candidature is to be considered for the vacancies, which were advertised for
an OBC category candidate; but when a candidate who though, otherwise
belongs to an OBC category candidate and has got marks in the TET lesser
than 60% of the cut off prescribed therein for the general category, in that
eventuality, the eligibility of the candidate irrespective of the fact, that she
belongs to an OBC category candidate, but then too the cut off marks
provided therein of 50% cannot be borrowed for the purposes to be applied,
when her candidature has been extended to be considered for the purposes of
a vacancy, which had been exclusively advertised for the general category
candidate and particularly, this fact has been sought to be argued by the
respondents counsel in the light of the fact, that this ambit of relaxation,
which has been provided by Clause 9, could have had been only exercised by
the State, by relaxing the eligibility criteria to be considered for appointment;
but since in the instant case there was no such relaxation clause, which was
provided by the State Government, in that eventuality, the petitioner had been
rightly ousted to be considered for appointment by inclusion of her name in
the merit list of 19.07.2018.
7. On the contrary, the contention of the learned counsel for the
petitioner is that the cut off of 50% marks, which has been normally
otherwise fixed for the OBC category candidates, would yet still be made
available to the petitioner, irrespective of the fact whether that she has applied
for against the general category vacancy, which was advertised, this argument
of the learned counsel for the petitioner, is not acceptable by this Court, for
the reason being, that the petitioner's submission of an application, itself was
obviously be presumed to be made after scrutinizing the terms of the
advertisement dated 03.01.2017 and it was with a conscious knowledge to
her, that her candidature is being extended to be considered for a general
category candidate only. In that eventuality, if at all her candidate was

5
required to be considered due to her placement in the merit list, it will not
eradicate or exclude the eligibility of procurement of 60% of marks in TET,
because in that eventuality the cut off marks of OBC category candidate of
50%, which the petitioner was having cannot, be borrowed to be applied in
the present circumstances, to over ride the eligibility of 60% cut off of TET
marks, which the general category candidate was under the norms required to
be possessed and particularly in the absence of there being any relaxation
provided by the State by issuing any necessary guidelines or circulars as
provided under Clause 9.
8. This is what has been laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court in
the judgment reported in (2017) 1 Supreme Court Case, 350 Vikas
Sankhala and Others vs. Vikas Kumar Aggarwal and Others in para 80,
81 and 82, wherein it has been observed, that power of relaxation of
eligibility criteria has been exclusively vested with the State Government; and
the relaxation from the minimum cut off marks of 60%, which has been
prescribed in the instant case for the general category candidate, could have
been equally made applicable even to the OBC category candidate, who
voluntarily applies to be consider her candidature against the general category
vacancy and it would be obviously only subject to the condition that the State
has relaxed the parameters. Since in the instant case there is no such
relaxation having being extended under para 9 of the relaxation, Clause for
TET marks, this Court is of the view that in the light of the parameters laid
down in para 80, 81 and 82 of the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court, which is
extracted hereunder:-, the petitioners contention for inclusion of her name in
the merit list of 19.07.2018, by treating her 50% marks in TET prescribed for
OBC, cannot be read and borrowed to be read in relation to 60% cut off
marks prescribed marks of TET for general category candidate, against which
she had applied.
"80. Having regard to the respective submissions noted above,
first aspect that needs consideration is as to whether relaxation in
TET pass marks would amount to concession in the recruitment
process. The High Court has held to be so on the premise that
para 9(a) dealing with such relaxation in TET marks forms part

6
of the document which relates to the recruitment procedure. It is
difficult to accept this rationale or analogy. Passing of TET
examination is a condition of eligibility for appointment as a
teacher. It is a necessary qualification without which a candidate
is not eligible to be considered for appointment. This was clearly
mentioned in guidelines/notification dated February 11, 2011.
These guidelines pertain to conducting of TET. Basic features
whereof have already been pointed out above. Even para 9 which
provides for concessions that can be given to certain reserved
categories deals with 'qualifying marks' that is to be obtained in
TET examination. Thus, a person who passes TET examination
becomes eligible to participate in the selection process as and
when such selection process for filling up of the posts of primary
teachers is to be undertaken by the State. On the other hand,
when it comes to recruitment of teachers, the method for
appointment of teachers is altogether different. Here, merit list of
successful candidates is to be prepared on the basis of marks
obtained under different heads. One of the heads is marks in
TET. So far as this head is concerned, 20% of the marks obtained
in TET are to be assigned to each candidate. Therefore, those
reserved category candidates who secured lesser marks in TET
would naturally get less marks under this head. We like to
demonstrate it with an example. Suppose a reserved category
candidate obtains 53 marks in TET, he is treated as having
qualified TET. However, when he is considered for selection to
the post of primary teacher, in respect of allocation of marks he
will get 20% marks for TET. As against him, a general candidate
who secures 70 marks in TET shall be awarded 14 marks in
recruitment process. Thus, on the basis of TET marks reserved
category candidate has not got any advantage while considering
his candidature for the post. On the contrary, "level playing field"
is maintained whereby a person securing higher marks in TET,
whether belonging to general category or reserved category, is
allocated higher marks in respect of 20% of TET marks. Thus, in
recruitment process no weightage or concession is given and
allocation of 20% of TET marks is applied across the board.
Therefore, the High Court is not correct in observing that
concession was given in the recruitment process on the basis of
relaxation in TET.
81. Once this vital differentiation is understood, it would lead to
the conclusion that no concession becomes available to the
reserved category candidate by giving relaxation in pass marks in
TET insofar as recruitment process is concerned. It only enables
them to compete with others by allowing them to participate in
the selection process. In this backdrop, irrespective of circular
dated May 11, 2011, the reserved category candidates who
secured more marks than marks obtained by the last candidate
selected in general category, would be entitled to be considered
against unreserved category vacancies. However, it would be

7
subject to the condition that these candidates have not availed
any other concession in terms of number of attempts, etc., except
on fee and age.
82. In Jitendra Kumar Singh and Anr. v. State of Uttar Pradesh,
this Court has very categorically held that relaxations given in
educational qualifications etc. making a person eligible to
participate in selection process would not be treated as availing
benefits in the recruitment/employment and the benefits
envisaged have to be those which have direct relation to
recruitment/employment and are relatable to the jovial
relationship of employer and employee. It is also clarified that
such benefits must occur from and should be post 'level playing
field'. We would like to reproduce the following discussion from
the said judgment touching upon the aforesaid aspects: (SCC pp.
138 & 146-47, para 48-49 & 75)
"48. In view of the aforesaid facts, we are of the
considered opinion that the submissions of the
Appellants that relaxation in fee or age would
deprive the candidates belonging to the reserved
category of an opportunity to compete against the
general category candidates is without any
foundation. It is to be noticed that the reserved
category candidates have not been given any
advantage in the selection process. All the candidates
had to appear in the same written test and face the
same interview. It is therefore quite apparent that the
concession in fee and age relaxation only enabled
certain candidates belonging to the reserved category
to fall within the zone of consideration. The
concession in age did not in any manner tilt the
balance in favour of the reserved category
candidates, in the preparation of final merit/select
list.
49. It is permissible for the State in view of Articles
14, 15, 16 and 38 of the Constitution of India to
make suitable provisions in law to eradicate the
disadvantages of candidates belonging to socially
and educationally backward classes. Reservations
are a mode to achieve the equality of opportunity
guaranteed Under Article 16(1) of the Constitution
of India. Concessions and relaxations in fee or age
provided to the reserved category candidates to
enable them to compete and seek benefit of
reservation, is merely an aid to reservation. The
concessions and relaxations place the candidates on
a par with general category candidates. It is only
thereafter the merit of the candidates is to be

8
determined without any further concessions in
favour of the reserved category candidates.
* * *
75. In our opinion, the relaxation in age does not in
any manner upset the "level playing field". It is not
possible to accept the submission of the learned
Counsel for the Appellants that relaxation in age or
the concession in fee would in any manner be
infringement of Article 16(1) of the Constitution of
India. These concessions are provisions pertaining to
the eligibility of a candidate to appear in the
competitive examination. At the time when the
concessions are availed, the open competition has
not commenced. It commences when all the
candidates who fulfill the eligibility conditions,
namely, qualifications, age, preliminary written test
and physical test are permitted to sit in the main
written examination. With age relaxation and the fee
concession, the reserved candidates are merely
brought within the zone of consideration, so that
they can participate in the open competition on
merit. Once the candidate participates in the written
examination, it is immaterial as to which category,
the candidate belongs. All the candidates to be
declared eligible had participated in the preliminary
test as also in the physical test. It is only thereafter
that successful candidates have been permitted to
participate in the open competition."
9. The petitioner's candidature cannot be included in the select list
of 19.07.2018, merely on the premise of borrowing the cut off marks of 50%
of TET for OBC category candidate, even if a person knowingly applies to
consider her/his candidature for vacancy, which has been exclusively limited
to be advertised for the general category candidate; because I am of the view
that if the candidate who applies for being considered against the general
category candidate and in the absence of there being a specific relaxation
granted by the State under Clause 9, the cut off percentage of marks of 60%,
which was otherwise mandatory to be available with the candidates, who had
extended his candidature to be considered against the general category
candidate; that would be equally made applicable even for the OBC category
candidate, who applies to be considered for general category candidates and
hence, non-inclusion of the petitioner's name in the select list of 19.07.2018,

9
do not suffer from any apparent vices or illegality as such which could call
for an interference under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
10. Thus, the writ petition fails and the same is accordingly dismissed.
 (Sharad Kumar Sharma, J.) 29.12.2021
